overview:
European Indology is the scholarly study of the languages, texts, religions, and histories of South Asia as it developed in Europe from the eighteenth century onward. It emerged at the intersection of colonial administration, missionary activity, philology, and philosophical curiosity, and gradually became a distinct academic discipline housed in universities and research institutes. While its earliest phases were closely tied to the needs of European empires, over time Indology diversified into critical textual scholarship, historical research, and, more recently, ethnographic and interdisciplinary approaches.

The "prehistory" of European Indology lies in Greco‑Roman reports about India, medieval travelogues, and early modern missionary accounts. In the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, figures such as Henry Thomas Colebrooke in Britain and French and German orientalists began systematic study of Sanskrit and other Indian languages, producing grammars, dictionaries, and translations. By the nineteenth century, Germany, France, and Britain had become major centers of Indological research, with universities establishing chairs in Sanskrit and comparative philology and libraries collecting large manuscript holdings from the subcontinent.

A hallmark of European Indology was its focus on philology and textual criticism. Scholars such as Albrecht Weber, Georg Bühler, Hermann Jacobi, and later generations edited and translated vast corpora of Sanskrit, Prakrit, and other regional texts. They developed methods for reconstructing critical editions from multiple manuscripts, tracing textual lineages, and situating works within broader literary and religious traditions. This philological orientation shaped the way Indian religions—including Jainism, Buddhism, and various Hindu traditions—were first presented to European audiences, often as systems distilled from canonical texts.

Within this broader field, the study of Jainism offers a clear example of European Indology’s impact and limitations. German Indologists like Weber and Jacobi, followed by Ernst Leumann, Walter Schubring, Ludwig Alsdorf, and others, used Jain manuscripts to demonstrate that Jainism was an independent religious‑philosophical tradition rather than a mere offshoot of Buddhism or Hinduism. They catalogued collections, produced editions of canonical texts, and analyzed doctrines such as non‑violence (ahiṃsā), karma, and the path to liberation. Italian scholars, including Francesco Lorenzo Pullè and later Indologists, contributed catalogues and studies of Jain narrative literature, embedding Jain studies within a wider European Indological network.

Over the twentieth century, European Indology expanded beyond its original textual core. Scholars began to integrate historical, sociological, and anthropological perspectives, examining how religious communities live, interpret, and transform their traditions over time. In Jain studies, for instance, researchers such as Paul Dundas and many others connected early canonical materials with medieval and modern practices, showing that Jain communities have complex histories rather than timeless doctrinal uniformity. At the same time, European Indology increasingly engaged with Indian scholars and institutions, moving from a one‑sided "discovery" narrative toward collaborative research.

Contemporary European Indology is both self‑critical and globally connected. It reassesses earlier orientalist frameworks, questions colonial power dynamics in manuscript collection and representation, and pays attention to regional languages, vernacular literatures, and lived religious practice. Indology now intersects with South Asian studies, religious studies, history, linguistics, and philosophy, and is practiced not only in Europe but worldwide. For Jainism and other Indian traditions, European Indology remains significant as a source of critical editions, historical studies, and comparative insights, yet it is increasingly complemented—and sometimes corrected—by scholarship rooted in South Asian academic and community contexts.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga-sūtra (as edited and translated in European Indology)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to early Jaina teachers; critical editions by Hermann Jacobi and others
primary_sources.original_text: णं च णं च णं च णं च णं च णं च
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇaṃ ca ṇaṃ ca ṇaṃ ca ṇaṃ ca ṇaṃ ca ṇaṃ ca
primary_sources.translation: "Again and again" (a repetitive phrase used in describing ascetic practice, here illustrative rather than a full passage).
primary_sources.notes: The Ācārāṅga-sūtra is one of the earliest Jain canonical texts, central to descriptions of monastic conduct and ascetic ideals. European Indologists, especially Hermann Jacobi, produced influential editions and translations based on multiple manuscripts, helping to establish Jainism as an independent religious tradition in academic discourse. Their work exemplifies the philological methods of European Indology—collating manuscripts, reconstructing a critical text, and providing annotated translations—while also shaping how Jain asceticism and ethics were first presented to European readers.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa-sūtra (European edited and translated versions)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu; edited and translated by various European Indologists
primary_sources.original_text: णमो अरिहंताणं, णमो सिद्धाणं, णमो आयरियाणं, णमो उवज्झायाणं, णमो लोए सव्वसाहूणं
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇamo arihaṃtāṇaṃ, ṇamo siddhāṇaṃ, ṇamo āyariyāṇaṃ, ṇamo uvajjhāyāṇaṃ, ṇamo loe savvasāhūṇaṃ
primary_sources.translation: "Homage to the Arhats, homage to the Siddhas, homage to the Ācāryas, homage to the Upādhyāyas, homage to all the Sādhus in the world."
primary_sources.notes: The Kalpa-sūtra, widely recited in Śvetāmbara Jain communities, contains biographies of the Tīrthaṅkaras and rules for monastic life. European Indologists edited and translated this text from manuscripts obtained in Indian libraries, making it one of the most accessible Jain scriptures in European languages. These editions influenced both academic understandings of Jain ritual and popular perceptions of Jainism, but they often prioritized a single sectarian recension and required later correction and contextualization by more nuanced historical and community-based studies.

primary_sources.title: Early European Indological catalogues of Jain manuscripts (e.g., Georg Bühler’s reports and Francesco Lorenzo Pullè’s catalogues)
primary_sources.author: Georg Bühler; Francesco Lorenzo Pullè; other nineteenth-century Indologists
primary_sources.notes: Nineteenth-century European Indologists compiled detailed catalogues of Jain manuscript collections in places such as Jaisalmer, Jaipur, and Florence. Georg Bühler’s reports on Jain libraries and Francesco Lorenzo Pullè’s "Catalogo dei manoscritti giainici" in Florence are representative examples. Although these catalogues are not primary religious texts, they are primary documentary sources for the history of European Indology: they record titles, languages, and conditions of manuscripts, document negotiations with Jain communities, and reveal how European scholars accessed and classified Jain literature. They also show the entanglement of scholarly interest with colonial and postcolonial power structures in the movement of manuscripts from local libraries to European institutions.

misconceptions.myth: European Indology is purely a colonial project that only served imperial interests and has no lasting scholarly value.
misconceptions.reality: European Indology did arise within colonial and missionary contexts, and its early phases were deeply shaped by imperial power relations. However, many Indologists also developed rigorous philological and historical methods that produced critical editions, grammars, and translations still used today. Contemporary scholars critically reassess orientalist biases while continuing to rely on and refine these textual tools, and they increasingly collaborate with South Asian academics and communities to create more balanced and context-sensitive studies.

misconceptions.myth: Indology only studies Sanskrit and ignores other Indian languages and non-Hindu traditions such as Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: Sanskrit was long the central focus of European Indology, but the discipline has also engaged with Prakrits, Pali, and numerous regional languages. Jain texts in Ardhamāgadhī and other Prakrits, as well as Buddhist and vernacular literatures, have been edited and translated by European scholars. While earlier work sometimes privileged Sanskritic and Brahmanical sources, later Indology and related South Asian studies have deliberately expanded to include Jain, Buddhist, and diverse regional traditions, correcting earlier imbalances.

misconceptions.myth: European Indologists presented Jainism as a static, timeless doctrine that has never changed.
misconceptions.reality: Some early Indological accounts did emphasize doctrinal continuity and treated Jainism as an unchanging system distilled from canonical texts. More recent scholarship, including work by historians and anthropologists, shows that Jain doctrines, practices, and institutions have evolved over centuries and vary across regions and sects. European Indology has itself diversified, incorporating historical and ethnographic approaches that highlight change, debate, and lived experience within Jain communities.

misconceptions.myth: Indology is an outdated discipline that has been completely replaced by modern South Asian studies.
misconceptions.reality: Indology has changed significantly, but it has not disappeared. Its core strengths—philology, textual criticism, and historical linguistics—remain essential for understanding premodern South Asian texts and intellectual traditions. Modern South Asian studies often build on Indological foundations while adding methods from history, anthropology, sociology, and religious studies. In practice, many scholars work at the intersection of these fields, combining close textual work with attention to contemporary social and religious life.
